passages.happening:
“Woe to the city of oppressors, rebellious and defiled!” (verse 1). She heeded no voice and accepted no correction; she does not trust in the LORD (verse 2). ‘Her princes are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves, leaving nothing for the morning’ (verse 3). Her prophets are reckless and faithless, and her priests profane the sanctuary and do violence to the law (verse 4). ‘The LORD within her is righteous; He does no wrong’ (verse 5); morning by morning he gives his justice, yet the unjust know no shame.

God has cut off nations and laid their cities waste (verse 6). He hoped Jerusalem would fear him and accept correction, but they were eager to do corrupt things (verse 7). So the people are to wait for the day he rises to testify, when he gathers the nations to pour out his anger, and the whole earth is consumed by the fire of his jealousy (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The corruption of verses 1 to 7 fits Jerusalem in the seventh century BC, shaped by Manasseh's long reign and before or during Josiah's reform. Every level of leadership is named: royal officials, judges, prophets and priests. Jeremiah, a younger contemporary, makes the same charges against the same classes.

The pictures come from a herding people's fears. Roaring lions, and wolves that hunt at dusk and leave nothing by morning, describe officials and judges who devour the vulnerable instead of protecting them. Against them stands the LORD in the city's midst, who gives justice every morning, like a faithful judge holding court at the gate each day.

Verse 6 reminds Jerusalem of what it had seen: Samaria's fall in 722 BC and Assyria's destruction of many cities. Jerusalem saw it and did not learn.
passages.later: Jeremiah made the same charge: ‘The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule by their own authority’ (Jeremiah 5:31). Ezekiel also pictured Jerusalem's officials as wolves tearing their prey (Ezekiel 22:27).
passages.asks: The LORD was in the city every morning, giving justice, while its leaders devoured the weak. Ask whether God's presence in your church or community is honored by how the weak are treated there. And ask what correction you have refused to accept.

passages.t: Pure lips, and a humble people
passages.happening:
‘For then I will restore pure lips to the peoples, that all may call upon the name of the LORD and serve Him shoulder to shoulder’ (verse 9). From beyond the rivers of Cush God's scattered worshipers will bring him an offering (verse 10).

On that day Jerusalem will not be put to shame for its wrongs, because God will remove the proud from among them (verse 11). ‘But I will leave within you a meek and humble people, and they will trust in the name of the LORD’ (verse 12). The remnant will not do wrong or tell lies, and they will feed and lie down with no one to make them afraid (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The fire of verse 8 consumes the earth, and then in verse 9 God purifies the lips of the peoples. Judgment in the prophets is often purifying rather than only destructive, like a refiner's fire that removes the waste from metal.

Pure lips may recall the tower of Babel, where the peoples' language was confused; here they are given clean speech to call on the LORD together. Shoulder to shoulder pictures the peoples serving God together.

The remnant is the humble who sought the LORD in 2:3. The proud are removed; the meek and humble are left, and they trust in the name of the LORD rather than in themselves.
passages.later: At Babel the LORD confused the language of the whole earth (Genesis 11:9). A psalm says, ‘The LORD sustains the humble’ (Psalm 147:6).
passages.asks: God promises a people who serve him shoulder to shoulder, from every nation. Ask who you serve alongside, and who you would rather not. And ask what it would mean for your own speech to be made pure.

passages.t: The LORD rejoices over you with singing
passages.happening:
“Sing for joy, O Daughter of Zion; shout aloud, O Israel! Be glad and rejoice with all your heart, O Daughter of Jerusalem!” (verse 14). ‘The LORD has taken away your punishment; He has turned back your enemy. Israel’s King, the LORD, is among you; no longer will you fear any harm’ (verse 15).

On that day Jerusalem will be told not to fear or let her hands hang limp (verse 16). ‘The LORD your God is among you; He is mighty to save. He will rejoice over you with gladness; He will quiet you with His love; He will rejoice over you with singing’ (verse 17).

God will gather those who grieve over the lost feasts (verse 18). He will deal with all who oppress them, ‘I will save the lame and gather the scattered’ (verse 19), and give them praise among all the peoples of the earth when he restores their fortunes before their eyes (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The book that began with God sweeping everything away ends with God singing. Zion is called to sing, and then God himself rejoices over his people with song. The King of Israel, the LORD, is in their midst, which was the promise of the temple and the covenant from the start.

Mighty to save is the language of a warrior who fights for his people. The lame and the scattered are gathered, as in Micah. Those once put to shame are given honor.

Some readers find the shift from chapter 1 to chapter 3 so sharp that they think the hopeful ending was added later, and many critical scholars hold that view for at least part of verses 14 to 20. Others argue that the move from judgment to restoration is typical of the prophets and fits Zephaniah's own logic.
passages.later: Micah has the same promise: ‘I will gather the lame; I will assemble the outcast’ (Micah 4:6). Zechariah gives a similar call: ‘Rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion’ (Zechariah 9:9).
passages.hard:
How can the same book announce the destruction of the earth and then promise joy and gathering?

Some readers find the shift from chapter 1 to chapter 3 so abrupt that they conclude the hopeful ending was added later by another hand, and many critical scholars hold that view for at least part of verses 14 to 20. Others argue that the move from judgment to restoration is typical of the prophets, as in Amos 9, Hosea 14 and Micah 7, and fits Zephaniah's own logic. The key is verses 8 and 9: the fire of God's jealousy consumes the earth, and then God purifies the lips of the peoples. Judgment in the prophets is often purifying rather than simply destructive, like a refiner's fire. The remnant that remains is the humble who sought the LORD in chapter 2.

On either view of how the book was put together, its final form teaches that God's judgment and his joy are not opposed. The God who will not ignore evil is the God who sings over his people.
passages.asks: God rejoices over his people with singing. Ask whether you believe God takes joy in you. And ask what fear he might be telling you to put down, so your hands no longer hang limp.
